verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal: the critic found that the objections based on a different reading of not valid do not hold. What remains is fixable. standards-compat-1 asks whether a stable branch can take a change that makes accepted updates fail. standards-compat-3 and maintenance-fit-3 ask which row-changing paths and cached plans the rewriter change covers. Message #3 is still unanswered, so a committer who knows this area has to decide whether this is a bug.

brief.title: Check not valid domain constraints on columns that update leaves unchanged
brief.problem: After `alter domain ... add constraint ... not valid`, an update that does not assign a new value to a domain column skips the check for that column, even when the old value violates the constraint. Insert does check not valid domain constraints, and so does an update that assigns a new literal. The author asks whether update should also check, citing an earlier remark by Álvaro Herrera.
brief.proposed_design: The rewriter checks each Var in the update target list. If its type is a domain with not valid constraints, it wraps the Var in a CoerceToDomain node. A column the statement does not mention gets a new resjunk target entry that does the same. The type cache gains a flag that records whether a domain has not valid constraints.
user_visible_surface: Update now fails when an unchanged domain column, or one set to itself, violates a not valid domain constraint.
Changed behaviour also covers `set c = c` and `set c = c::d1`.
author_claims: Insert already checks not valid domain constraints, so the gap exists only for update.
Álvaro Herrera raised the same point in an earlier thread.
brief.thread_state: Chao Li replied that the current behaviour is arguably correct, because not valid means existing bad data is tolerated while unchanged, and asked for other opinions. He also gave code comments in case it is agreed to be a bug; the author has not replied, and nobody has settled whether this is a bug.
unclear: The proposal does not say why the check should apply to columns the update does not assign, given what not valid means.
The proposal does not say whether the same rule applies to not valid table check constraints, which update does not recheck on unchanged columns.
The proposal does not say how it handles merge, insert on conflict do update, or updates through views and triggers.
The proposal does not measure the cost of extra domain checks on every updated row.
The CommitFest entry targets backport, but the thread does not discuss changing behaviour in stable branches.
search_queries: alter domain add constraint not valid

objections.title: Backporting turns working updates into errors after a minor upgrade
objections.failure_scenario: A site has a domain with a not valid constraint and old rows that violate it, and its application runs `update ... set status = ...` on those rows. After a minor upgrade the patch makes those updates fail, even though they never touch the domain column. The site learns this from production errors, with no setting to restore the old behaviour.
objections.argument: The CommitFest entry is tagged Backport and Bugfix with target version stable, but the thread has not agreed that the current behaviour is a bug. Message #3 argues it is the intended meaning of not valid, and nobody answered. Stable branches normally do not take changes that make previously accepted statements fail unless the old behaviour is wrong. The patch prose has no release-note or documentation hunk that explains the change.
objections.author_must_show: Why is this a bug fix that is safe for stable branches, and not a behaviour change for master only, given the disagreement in message #3?

critic.reasoning: The entry targets stable, and the thread has not agreed this is a bug. The `alter domain` documentation says updated rows are always checked, which supports the bug reading, but a minor release would still make accepted updates fail.

objections.title: Rule covers update in the rewriter but not other row-changing paths
objections.failure_scenario: After the patch, `update dt1 set i = i + 1` fails on a violating row. A `merge ... when matched then update set i = i + 1` or `insert ... on conflict do update set i = excluded.i` on the same row may still succeed, and so may a before trigger that changes the row. Users find that the same row change is accepted by one statement and rejected by another.
objections.argument: Message #2 describes the change only in rewriteTargetListIU for update target lists. The material does not say whether merge, on conflict do update, updatable views, or rows changed by before triggers get the same check. If the goal is consistency with insert, a partial rule replaces one inconsistency with several.
objections.author_must_show: Do merge, on conflict do update, updatable views and before-trigger changes all apply the same not valid domain check, and is there a test for each?

critic.reasoning: Merge actions and `on conflict do update` target lists also pass through rewriteTargetListIU, so they may be covered. The material does not confirm this, and rows changed by before triggers do not pass through the rewriter.

objections.title: Rewriter hook every update-producing path must remember
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch adds or changes a path that builds update target lists, such as merge or insert on conflict do update, and does not call the new wrapping step. Rows pass in one path and fail in another, and no test fails until a user reports the difference. A prepared update cached before `alter domain ... not valid` may also skip the check.
objections.argument: Message #2 places the check in rewriteTargetListIU by adding resjunk entries for unmentioned columns. The proposal does not say how merge, on conflict, views or trigger-changed rows are covered, or whether cached plans are invalidated when the domain flag changes. It also adds a type cache lookup per domain column per update and per-row checks, with no measurement.
objections.author_must_show: Which update paths does this cover, how are cached plans invalidated after the constraint is added, and what does it cost per row?

critic.reasoning: The cost falls only on domains that have not valid constraints, which weakens the performance part. The proposal does not say whether a cached update plan is rebuilt after `alter domain ... not valid`, since the old plan has no CoerceToDomain node.

objections.title: New TypeCacheEntry field conflicts with a stable-branch target
objections.failure_scenario: An extension is compiled against a minor release and reads TypeCacheEntry fields from lookup_type_cache(). If a backported patch changes the struct layout, that extension reads the wrong fields after the server is updated, and the problem shows up only at run time.
objections.argument: The patch touches src/include/utils/typcache.h, and the brief says it adds a flag to the type cache. Extensions use TypeCacheEntry, and the entry targets stable branches. The proposal does not say how the new field keeps the ABI stable in back branches.
objections.author_must_show: If this is backpatched, how does the TypeCacheEntry change keep the layout that already-built extensions rely on?

critic.reasoning: The patch touches typcache.h and the entry targets stable branches. A field added at the end of TypeCacheEntry is the usual safe form, but the material does not show where the field goes.

refuted.title: New not valid contract is not defined or documented
refuted.failure_scenario: A user reads the `alter domain` documentation and adds a not valid constraint, planning to clean up old rows over time. Every update to those rows, even ones that change only other columns, now fails. The user cannot fix rows one column at a time and finds out only when updates error.
refuted.argument: The patch touches only rewriteHandler.c, typcache.c and the regression tests, so the `alter domain` and `update` documentation do not describe the new rule. Message #1 asks whether the four statements should fail but does not state the rule that decides it. Message #3 gives a different reading of not valid. Without a written contract that states what is checked on update and why, later patches cannot tell which reading to follow.
refuted.author_must_show: What exact rule should the `alter domain` documentation state for when update rechecks a not valid domain constraint, and how does it match table check constraints?

critic.reasoning: The `alter domain` documentation already says newly inserted or updated rows are always checked against all constraints, even not valid ones. Table check constraints follow the same rule, so the proposal has a written contract to follow.

refuted.title: Backport would make existing updates fail after a minor upgrade
refuted.failure_scenario: A site added a domain constraint with not valid and left old rows that violate it. After a minor release, its application runs `update dt1 set i = i + 1` on those rows, and the update now fails with a domain check error. Nothing changed in the schema, so the site only learns about it in production.
refuted.argument: The CommitFest entry is tagged Backport and Bugfix with target version stable, but no message discusses stable branches. Message #3 argues that the current behaviour may be correct, so this is not an agreed bug. Data already stored in the old form would turn into a hard error on update with no warning, and that is a behaviour change, which stable branches normally avoid.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should a minor release start rejecting updates on rows that the current release accepts, rather than making this change in master only?

refuted.title: Behaviour change proposed for backport to stable branches
refuted.failure_scenario: A site added a not valid domain constraint and planned to clean old rows later. After a minor-release upgrade, a routine `update ... set status = ...` starts failing on rows whose domain column it never touches. The application breaks in production with no schema change on its side.
refuted.argument: The CommitFest entry is tagged Backport and Bugfix and targets stable, but the thread has not agreed that this is a bug. Message #3 argues the current behaviour is correct, and nobody replied. Stricter checks in a minor release turn a semantic choice into an outage for users who relied on the documented meaning of not valid.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is this a bug fix suitable for stable branches rather than a behaviour change for the next major release only?

refuted.title: Special case for domains, unlike not valid table check constraints
refuted.failure_scenario: A user has a not valid check constraint on a table column and a not valid check on a domain column with the same rule. An update that leaves both columns unchanged fails for the domain column and passes for the table column. The user cannot predict from the docs which one holds.
refuted.argument: The proposal compares update only with insert, which checks new values in both cases. Table check constraints marked not valid are not rechecked on unchanged columns, and the proposal does not say whether that rule should change too. One rule for not valid in two places is easier to document and to keep correct.
refuted.author_must_show: Should not valid table check constraints also be rechecked on unchanged columns, and if not, why do domains need a different rule?

critic.reasoning: Postgres evaluates every table check constraint, including not valid ones, on the new row of each update, whichever columns changed. An update of a violating row already fails for tables, so the proposal brings domains in line with them.

refuted.title: The change breaks the main use of not valid domain constraints
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA adds `check(value <> 2) not valid` to a domain so new data obeys the rule while old rows are fixed over time. The application keeps running `update ... set i = i + 1` on old rows. After this change, and after a minor release if it is backported, those updates fail in production on columns the statement never touched.
refuted.argument: Users choose not valid so that existing rows stay usable until `validate constraint` runs, and message #3 reads it that way. The proposal moves the cost onto those users: every update of an old row now fails until the data is clean. Message #1 asks whether this should error but gives no user who wants it. Table check constraints do not recheck unchanged columns on update, so this would also make domains behave unlike tables.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users want updates of unrelated columns to fail on rows that break a not valid domain constraint, and what should they do before they can validate?

critic.reasoning: The argument rests on table check constraints not rechecking unchanged columns, but they do recheck the whole new row on every update. The documented rule for not valid already says updated rows are checked, so users of table constraints have this behaviour today.

refuted.title: No user report shows the current behaviour causes a problem
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer pushes this as a bug fix and a minor release changes update behaviour for every database that uses not valid domain constraints. Nobody asked for the change, and the first reports come from users whose updates start to fail.
refuted.argument: Message #1 is a question, "should UPDATE statement need to verify", and links one earlier remark with no user case behind it. The thread has no -bugs or -general report, no production story, and no comparison with other systems. The only reply, message #3, says the current behaviour is arguably correct. In four CommitFests nobody has argued for the change on the list.
refuted.author_must_show: Which user reports or real workloads show harm from update skipping not valid domain checks on unchanged columns?

critic.reasoning: Its failure scenario duplicates standards-compat-1. User demand is a weak test for a change that makes update follow the documented rule that updated rows are always checked.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a flag to TypeCacheEntry in src/include/utils/typcache.h, which extensions read.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Backporting turns working updates into errors after a minor upgrade

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: The rewriter adds CoerceToDomain nodes and resjunk target entries, so update plans and cached plans change.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The CommitFest entry is tagged Backport and targets stable, and the change makes accepted updates fail.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The check lives in rewriteTargetListIU, so every path that changes rows must go through it or repeat it.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Update rewrite looks up the type cache for domain columns, and affected rows get an extra domain check.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Why is this a bug fix that is safe for stable branches, and not a change for master only, given the unanswered disagreement in message #3?
Which documented rule supports checking a not valid domain constraint on columns the update does not assign, in reply to message #3?
Do merge, insert on conflict do update, updatable views and rows changed by before triggers all get the same check, and is each tested?
Is a cached update plan rebuilt after `alter domain ... add constraint ... not valid`, so that it gains the CoerceToDomain node?
If this is backpatched, where does the new TypeCacheEntry field go so that already-built extensions keep a valid struct layout?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the rewriter target-list code and domain constraint handling in the type cache. No committer has posted in the thread; one only moved the CommitFest entry.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a behaviour change in update, possibly in stable branches, where sites with violating rows see new errors after a minor upgrade. The owner also signs for coverage of every row-changing path, with no end date.
committability.author_follow_up: The author moved the entry forward in December 2025 but has not answered message #3, and the patch has needed a rebase since April 2026.

priority.reason: Only sites with not valid domain constraints and violating rows are affected, and the patch is small but changes the rewriter and a type cache struct. The entry has sat through four CommitFests because nobody qualified has said whether this is a bug.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review cannot tell which paths reach the new wrapping step, where the TypeCacheEntry field sits, or whether the flag is reset when the type cache is invalidated. The statement that the documentation supports the change comes from the critic, not from the thread.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: CHECK constraint deferrable Support
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets CHECK constraints be declared DEFERRABLE and INITIALLY DEFERRED, as the SQL standard allows, so SET CONSTRAINTS can delay a CHECK until commit. Rows that fail a deferrable CHECK are rechecked at commit time.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the CHECK implementation assumes constraints are immutable, and the patch does not change that assumption, so he called the feature a toy. Others then argued it should be dropped or combined with deferrable NOT NULL, which Robert Haas and Vik Fearing disputed. Dean Rasheed also reported open bugs, including a deferred constraint that still failed immediately and a wrong constraint-exclusion result. The visible messages do not show why the author withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I continue to assert that basing this feature on the current CHECK implementation will produce nothing but a toy feature, that's not only of little practical use but will be an active foot-gun for people who expect it to do more than it can.

precedents_retrieved.title: Track invalidation_reason in pg_replication_slots.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Track invalidation_reason in pg_replication_slots.
Reverted commit(s): Track conflict_reason in pg_replication_slots.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Till now, the reason for replication slot invalidation is not tracked
directly in pg_replication_slots. A recent commit 007693f2a3 added
'conflict_reason' to show the reasons for slot conflict/invalidation, but
only for logical slots.

This commit adds a new column 'invalidation_reason' to show invalidation
reasons for both physical and logical slots. And, this commit also turns
'conflict_reason' text column to 'conflicting' boolean column (effectively
reverting commit 007693f2a3). The 'conflicting' column is true for
invalidation reasons 'rows_removed' and 'wal_level_insufficient' because
those make the slot conflict with recovery. When 'conflicting' is true,
one can now look at the new 'invalidation_reason' column for the reason
for the logical slot's conflict with recovery.

The new 'invalidation_reason' column will also be useful to track other
invalidation reasons in the future commit.

precedents_retrieved.title: Reimplement targetlist SRFs using ROWS FROM ()
precedents_retrieved.summary: Andres Freund proposed removing set-returning functions in the target list (tSRFs) from generic expression evaluation by rewriting them in the planner into ROWS FROM () function RTEs joined laterally. The patch series also dropped the least-common-multiple row count rule, removed materialization from nodeFunctionscan.c, added syntax for returning a record unexpanded, and forbade SRFs in UPDATE, ORDER BY and GROUP BY.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the LATERAL rewrite added about 500 lines of hard-to-read planner code and could lock in incompatibilities. He drafted a planner prototype that evaluates tSRFs in a Result-like pipeline node, and both authors agreed to continue that way. He also objected that skipping materialization gives wrong results on rescan, for example inside a nestloop, and that forbidding SRFs in ORDER BY was arbitrary. Michael Paquier then returned the entry with feedback because of low activity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: But it's now looking to me like the latter would be a lot simpler from the point of view of planner complexity, and in particular from the point of view of proving correctness (equivalence of the query transformation).

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow AddForeignUpdateTargets to add extra target expressions other than columns
precedents_retrieved.summary: postgres_fdw identifies remote rows for non-direct UPDATE and DELETE by ctid alone, so when the remote table is partitioned or has inheritance children, rows in other children with the same ctid are also changed. The patch lets AddForeignUpdateTargets add extra target expressions that are not columns, implemented as Params that carry the remote tableoid up to ModifyTable, so the remote statement can also filter on tableoid.
precedents_retrieved.objection: An earlier approach that expanded the tuple descriptor with junk columns was dropped. Etsuro Fujita said it broke the planner assumption that rel->max_attr matches the catalog and could slow down foreign scans. The Param-based patch then drew a review comment from Tom Lane, shown only as a quote, suggesting that FDWs be allowed to define extra system column IDs instead. Fujita agreed with that comment but found no clear way to implement it, did not have time in the v13 cycle, and marked the entry Returned with feedback after it had waited on author for several commitfests.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I 100% agree with Tom, and actually, I tried to address his comments, but I haven't come up with a clear solution for that yet.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rewrite the code in a different language
precedents_retrieved.summary: Joel Jacobson asked whether Postgres could be ported from C to Rust, with a tool that converts every upstream commit automatically. The Rust port would follow the master branch until all developers moved to Rust.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas argued that C is the canonical language for system software and has a large, stable ecosystem. He did not want a project meant to last 20 more years tied to a young language, or to one controlled by one company. Joshua D. Drake said that no language other than C meets the needs for performance, stability, maturity and portability. Later replies suggested writing extensions in Rust instead of rewriting the core.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: But if I were starting a database project that I hoped or expected to last another 20 years, I'm not sure I'd want to be tied to a language with less than 10 years of history.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix permission tests for views/tables proven empty by constraint exclusion.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Fix permission tests for views/tables proven empty by constraint exclusion.
Reverted commit(s): Add regression test for bug fixed by recent refactoring.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
A view defined as "select <something> where false" had the curious property
that the system wouldn't check whether users had the privileges necessary
to select from it.  More generally, permissions checks could be skipped
for tables referenced in sub-selects or views that were proven empty by
constraint exclusion (although some quick testing suggests this seldom
happens in cases of practical interest).  This happened because the planner
failed to include rangetable entries for such tables in the finished plan.

This was noticed in connection with erroneous handling of materialized
views, but actually the issue is quite unrelated to matviews.  Therefore,
revert commit 200ba1667b3a8d7a9d559d2f05f83d209c9d8267 in favor of a more
direct test for the real problem.

Back-patch to 9.2 where the bug was introduced (by commit
7741dd6590073719688891898e85f0cb73453159).

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the corpus search returned no earlier proposal on this or a similar idea. Message #1 points to an earlier remark by Álvaro Herrera on the same point, but the thread shows nothing of what it said or how it ended, so no prior-rejection objection can be raised.
Objections raised; pg_dump round-trip is not affected because the proposal adds no object or syntax.

The proposal adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog column or protocol change. The new type cache flag lives only in backend memory. The only concerns from this angle are the stable-branch target and the header change.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect beyond what domain check constraints already have: the same check expressions already run on insert and on update of assigned columns. More updates may fail or run checks, but no role gains a new ability, and no data becomes visible to anyone new.

The proposal changes how update treats existing domain values under a not valid constraint, and no existing feature or extension makes update do that. `alter domain ... validate constraint` checks existing data, but it rejects the whole statement if old rows violate the constraint. Whether update should check unchanged columns is a question of semantics, raised in message #3, and other angles cover it.
Two objections apply; the precedent search found no related earlier proposal.
